WITH run AS (
  SELECT domain_id
  FROM runs
  WHERE id = $1::bigint
)
-- The first node after the trigger, and the shape the parent design fixes for every
-- workflow in this set (.specs/2026-08-19-research-pipeline-port.md, section 4): the
-- domain's personas and taxonomy, read as ONE query answering exactly one row. Both
-- halves of that are claims about this statement rather than house style, and both
-- are readable off it.

-- ONE QUERY, because the alternative is a lookup node per list, and a lookup node is
-- a second branch that races whatever reads it. What is fetched is small by
-- construction: a domain's personas, categories, terms and criteria are rows an
-- operator wrote, so taking them together costs one round trip and nothing else.

-- ONE ROW, because a Postgres node maps its statement over the items it was handed
-- and passes on what the statement returned. A SELECT matching nothing returns no
-- row, the node emits no item, and every node below it is then skipped with nothing
-- written anywhere: the pass ends looking exactly like a pass that found no work.
-- That is the failure this shape exists to make impossible. The outer SELECT names
-- no FROM at all, so it produces one row whatever the database holds, and every list
-- is a scalar subquery COALESCEd to an empty JSON array.

-- Which leaves one thing for every node below to be careful about. An empty list
-- here is a measured empty, an unresolvable run is not, and the two arrive spelled
-- the same way. domain_id is the discriminator and the only one: NULL when the run
-- id matched no row, a real id when the domain simply states no terms. Read it
-- before reading a length.

-- run_id is the parameter rather than a column read back, so it survives a run id
-- that resolves to nothing. It has to travel because this node's answer REPLACES the
-- item the trigger was handed: whatever the dispatcher sent is gone past here, and
-- the run is what a ledger row and the closing update are charged to.

-- Every list is ordered, which nothing downstream requires and every reader benefits
-- from: two passes over one unchanged domain hand the nodes below the same lists in
-- the same order, so a diff between two runs is about the documents rather than
-- about the order a planner happened to return rows in.
SELECT
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  (SELECT domain_id FROM run) AS domain_id,

  -- The domain row, cut to the members the nodes below read. feature_version is the
  -- one that has to travel: the feature group holds each document's composed version
  -- against the domain's, and fetching one integer separately is the lookup node
  -- this shape exists to avoid. NULL rather than an empty object when the run id
  -- resolved to nothing, which is the same discriminator domain_id carries.
  (SELECT jsonb_build_object(
     'id', d.id,
     'slug', d.slug,
     'name', d.name,
     'settings', d.settings,
     'feature_version', d.feature_version,
     'embedding_model', d.embedding_model)
     FROM domains d
    WHERE d.id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)) AS domain,

  -- The personas. system_text is operator-owned prose and is the trusted half of
  -- what prompt-frame.ts composes around an untrusted chunk; nothing in this
  -- workflow writes it, and no node below may put a document's text where a persona
  -- belongs.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', p.id,
       'role', p.role,
       'system_text', p.system_text)
       ORDER BY p.role, p.id)
       FROM personas p
      WHERE p.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS personas,

  -- The categories, which are the buckets the terms below are filed under. key
  -- rather than id is what a reader downstream matches on: features.ts builds a
  -- column name out of it and static-gate.ts groups hits by it, so the surrogate
  -- id travels for an operator's benefit and the key is what the libraries read.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', c.id,
       'key', c.key,
       'name', c.name,
       'parent_id', c.parent_id)
       ORDER BY c.key, c.id)
       FROM categories c
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS categories,

  -- The terms, joined to their category's key rather than carrying category_id.
  -- Four members and this exact spelling, because three libraries read this one
  -- list and each reads a different subset of it: static-gate.ts takes pattern,
  -- weight and polarity, features.ts takes pattern and category, and
  -- feature-version.ts takes all four. A term list selected without the join
  -- satisfies the first reader and starves the other two, with nothing failing.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'category', c.key,
       'pattern', t.pattern,
       'weight', t.weight,
       'polarity', t.polarity)
       ORDER BY c.key, t.pattern, t.id)
       FROM terms t
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = t.category_id
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS terms,

  -- The criteria, joined to their category the same way. Nothing in this workflow
  -- reads them: they are ar-score's subject, and the group that closes this pass
  -- hands that workflow the findings to score rather than this context, so it
  -- fetches its own. They are selected here because the design fixes the taxonomy as
  -- what this node fetches, and the taxonomy is these three tables, so a node group
  -- added below reads them without a second lookup and without a second branch to
  -- reason about.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', k.id,
       'category', c.key,
       'value', k.value,
       'kind', k.kind)
       ORDER BY c.key, k.kind, k.id)
       FROM criteria k
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = k.category_id
      WHERE k.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS criteria

SELECT
-- One row per source, and every node group below this one is built on that. A
-- Postgres node maps its statement over the items it was handed and passes on what
-- the statement returned, so this node takes the one context item above it and
-- answers as many items as the domain has sources worth reading. An HTTP Request node
-- runs once per input item, so a pass over four sources makes four requests because
-- this statement answered four rows, and nothing below it has to loop.

-- Which also means this node's answer REPLACES the context item, the way that item
-- replaced the one the trigger was handed. The personas and the taxonomy are not
-- gone, but they are no longer in $json: a node below reaches them as $('Load Domain
-- Context').first().json, for the same reason ar-dispatch's Invoke Target Workflow
-- reads its workflow id off Plan Dispatch rather than off the item the Postgres node
-- in front of it wrote. run_id is the exception and is echoed into every row from the
-- parameter, because a ledger row and a closing update are charged to the run rather
-- than to a source.

-- Two parameters, in declaration order: the run and the domain, both read off that
-- one item. Neither is asked of the database again here. The pair came out of a
-- single read of the runs row a moment ago, so a second lookup would re-read a row
-- nothing has changed, and deriving the domain a second way is how the two start
-- being able to disagree.

-- One SELECT over one table, and that is a property of this schema rather than of the
-- statement. The design this one is ported from held a feed's configuration in a
-- hand-written module and its cursor in a table of its own, so the equivalent read
-- joined what a person had edited to what a run had written, and adding a feed meant
-- a deploy. Here everything that varies per feed is a column on the row: the whole of
-- a source is one row, and this is the whole of the selection.

-- Eleven of the twelve columns, and enabled is the omission. It is the WHERE clause's
-- business rather than a reader's below: a row that reached this projection is
-- enabled by construction, and carrying the column onward is an invitation to branch
-- on it a second time.

  $1::bigint AS run_id,

  -- Which feed this is and how to reach it. kind is what selects the adapter for the
  -- row, and the two ids are what a document written from this source is filed under.
  -- endpoint is NOT NULL and may still be empty, which is a source somebody has not
  -- finished configuring rather than one that needs no address.
  s.id AS source_id,
  s.domain_id,
  s.kind,
  s.endpoint,

  -- The arrangement, from both of its ends: how to read this source, and what a
  -- correct reading of it looks like. Data the parse engine is directed by, and never
  -- anything it evaluates, which is what keeps adding a feed an INSERT. Both default
  -- to an empty object, so a source nobody has configured yet arrives here shaped
  -- like every other one and the adapter's own defaults apply.
  s.parser_config,
  s.contract,

  -- Where the last fetch stopped, in whatever spelling the adapter that wrote it
  -- chose. NULL means this source has never been fetched, or that its adapter keeps
  -- no cursor at all. It stays NULL rather than becoming an empty string, which an
  -- adapter would hand back to its source as a real position.
  s.cursor,

  -- The four members src/lib/source-health.ts reads, selected here so the health node
  -- group can work a source's next counters out of the item it already holds rather
  -- than out of a second SELECT. flagged is in that list even though the WHERE clause
  -- below has already fixed it at false: reading it off the row keeps the library's
  -- input a reading, where a Code node restating the constant would be this
  -- statement's own predicate written down a second time, somewhere it can stop
  -- agreeing.
  s.consecutive_failures,
  s.last_success_at,
  s.last_failure_at,
  s.flagged
FROM sources s
-- enabled AND NOT flagged, and the sticky note beside this node carries the argument
-- for why those are two columns rather than one. What belongs on the statement is
-- that both are NOT NULL with a default, so this predicate partitions the domain's
-- sources rather than quietly dropping the rows whose flag was never set: a nullable
-- boolean compares UNKNOWN, and a row that is neither selected nor excluded is the
-- one nobody goes looking for.
WHERE s.domain_id = $2::bigint
  AND s.enabled
  AND NOT s.flagged
-- A NULL domain_id selects nothing, which is where a pass started by hand ends: no
-- request is made and no row is written anywhere. Three different situations reach
-- zero rows here and this statement parts none of them, those being no run behind the
-- id, a domain with no sources, and a domain whose sources are all switched off or
-- flagged. domain_id on the context item is the discriminator, which is why Load
-- Domain Context answers one row whatever the database holds and this node does not
-- have to.

-- Ordered by id, which nothing below requires and every reader benefits from, for the
-- reason the lists in the node above are ordered: two passes over one unchanged
-- domain hand the nodes below the same sources in the same order.
ORDER BY s.id

WITH
-- Where a reading becomes a row, and the keep half of fail-flag-keep written as one
-- statement. A reading its contract refused is stored with the reason it was refused
-- rather than dropped, so a source whose shape has moved leaves evidence behind
-- instead of a fall in volume that reads exactly like a quiet week.

-- Extract Records decided the parse and nothing here revisits it. parse_status and
-- parse_error arrive as parameters and are written as they came: the contract was
-- read up there, beside the config that directed the reading, and a second judgment
-- down here would be a copy with nothing comparing it against the first.

-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever happened. The insert sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT names
-- no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was handed. A
-- reading that was written, a repeat capture that was not, and an item carrying no
-- reading at all each answer one row, which is what lets the health group below pair
-- its input against Extract Records by index, the same pairing Extract Records makes
-- against the fetch. Select Active Sources is reached differently, its rows being one
-- per source where these items are one per reading: the health group gathers the
-- readings under the source id each of them carries. An INSERT ... RETURNING on its
-- own emits nothing for a conflict, and the item would then vanish from the stream at
-- exactly the point where a repeat capture is the ordinary outcome.

-- Seven parameters, in declaration order: the run, the domain, the source, the
-- reading, the entry it was read from, and the two columns the parse answered. The
-- two JSONB members travel as the text JSON.stringify made of them, because the
-- payload of a url or an rss source is one whole document rather than an object, and
-- a bare string is not JSON until something encodes it.

-- The whitespace run the hash basis collapses, spelled out rather than left to the
-- shorthand class. Postgres reads that shorthand as ASCII whitespace and JavaScript
-- reads it, under the u flag, as the Unicode set, so the two disagree about a
-- non-breaking space and about a byte order mark sitting inside a body.
-- src/sources/listing-api.ts computes the same digest Node side and both writers
-- share one unique key, so a class differing by a single code point is two rows for
-- one item on every source that is reached both ways.
whitespace AS (
  SELECT '[\u0009\u000a\u000b\u000c\u000d\u0020\u00a0\u1680'
      || '\u2000\u2001\u2002\u2003\u2004\u2005\u2006\u2007'
      || '\u2008\u2009\u200a\u2028\u2029\u202f\u205f\u3000'
      || '\ufeff]+' AS run
),

-- The parameters, cast once. Both JSONB members arrive as JSON text, so a JavaScript
-- null arrives as the JSON null literal rather than as SQL NULL, and nullif is what
-- puts the two absences back together. documents.raw draws that distinction in its
-- own comment: NULL says no payload was ever stored, where a JSON null would claim
-- the source answered and answered with nothing.
candidate AS (
  SELECT
    $2::bigint AS domain_id,
    $3::bigint AS source_id,
    nullif($4::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS record,
    nullif($5::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS raw,
    $6::text AS parse_status,
    $7::text AS parse_error
),

-- The two columns a documents row takes from the reading, read off the field map by
-- name. url and body are the field names both adapters under src/sources/ write, and
-- that convention is the whole of the mapping: naming a field map's members after the
-- columns costs an operator one sentence of documentation, where a second mapping
-- from field names to column names would be another config to get wrong, and getting
-- it wrong would produce documents with no body and nothing to say why.

-- A member that is not a string is not text whatever it coerced to, so a numeric url
-- reads as no url rather than as a link to a number. The empty string is an absence
-- for url, which is NULL where there is no such place and never '', and a value for
-- body, which is NOT NULL and may still be empty: a capture that yielded no text was
-- kept anyway, which is the rule this whole statement is named after.

-- The WHERE clause is what confines this statement to readings. An item carrying no
-- record is a source that answered nothing on this pass, and that is a fact about the
-- source rather than a document: nothing is inserted, the outer SELECT still answers
-- its one row, and the health group below is what records that the fetch happened and
-- came back with nothing to read. What that costs is the payload, which reaches no
-- column and does not survive the pass. Storing it would put rows in the corpus that
-- no reader of the corpus wants, since every one of them treats a row as an item that
-- was captured rather than as a fetch that was attempted.
reading AS (
  SELECT
    c.domain_id,
    c.source_id,
    c.raw,
    c.parse_status,
    c.parse_error,
    nullif(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(c.record -> 'url') = 'string'
                THEN c.record ->> 'url'
           END, '') AS url,
    COALESCE(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(c.record -> 'body') = 'string'
                  THEN c.record ->> 'body'
             END, '') AS body
  FROM candidate c
  WHERE c.record IS NOT NULL
),

-- The content hash, and the key one row per distinct item stands on. The basis is the
-- url and the body, each with its whitespace runs collapsed and its ends trimmed,
-- JSON encoded into a two member array so that the halves cannot bleed into each
-- other: without the encoding a url ending in the first words of a body would collide
-- with a shorter url and a longer one.

-- What is left OUT of the basis is the half that does the work. The source is not in
-- it, deliberately, because documents.hash exists so that capturing the same item
-- from a second source lands on the row already there rather than beside it. Neither
-- is the run, nor the day, nor the domain.

-- Byte for byte the digest src/sources/listing-api.ts computes, and the agreement is
-- measured rather than asserted: the same hash over the same JSON encoding of the
-- same collapsed pair. Nothing fails when the two drift apart. The corpus doubles
-- instead.
hashed AS (
  SELECT
    r.domain_id,
    r.source_id,
    r.raw,
    r.parse_status,
    r.parse_error,
    r.url,
    r.body,
    encode(sha256(convert_to(
      '[' || to_json(collapsed.url)::text
          || ',' || to_json(collapsed.body)::text || ']',
      'UTF8')), 'hex') AS hash
  FROM reading r
  CROSS JOIN whitespace ws
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT
      btrim(regexp_replace(COALESCE(r.url, ''), ws.run, ' ', 'g'), ' ') AS url,
      btrim(regexp_replace(r.body, ws.run, ' ', 'g'), ' ') AS body) AS collapsed
),

-- The write. DO NOTHING is what makes a repeat capture write no second row, and the
-- conflict target is the constraint by NAME rather than the column list, so renaming
-- the constraint breaks this statement instead of quietly arbitrating on something
-- else. documents.hash carries the argument for why the column is NOT NULL as well as
-- UNIQUE: a nullable member would leave this clause never firing at all, with the
-- insert reporting success and the corpus gaining a copy per pass.

-- parse_status is written rather than left to its default. The column defaults to ok
-- and its own comment says exactly what that default cannot tell apart, being a
-- document that parsed from one whose writer never set the column. This writer always
-- knows which, so it says which, and a NULL reaching here is Extract Records
-- contradicting itself rather than an absence for a default to fill. NOT NULL is what
-- reports it, loudly, which is the right volume for a state that cannot happen.

-- What a repeat capture does NOT do is correct the row already standing. The stored
-- row keeps the first reading's status and its error. Content that hashes the same
-- cannot have diverged differently unless the contract itself moved, and moving a
-- contract is an operator's edit whose re-parse is a pass of its own rather than
-- something to smuggle in behind a dedupe.
written AS (
  INSERT INTO documents (
    domain_id, source_id, hash, url, body, raw, parse_status, parse_error)
  SELECT
    h.domain_id, h.source_id, h.hash, h.url, h.body, h.raw,
    h.parse_status, h.parse_error
  FROM hashed h
  ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT documents_hash_unique DO NOTHING
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and it is about the write rather than about the parse.
-- The reading, its warnings, the config faults and the HTTP status all stay on
-- Extract Records' items, which the health group reads back by name and a node below
-- can too. Restating any of them in this projection would be a second copy able to
-- disagree with the first, and the three ids below are here because a ledger row and
-- the closing update are charged to the run rather than to a source.

-- document_id is the row this reading is in, whether or not this pass is what put it
-- there. COALESCE reads it out of the insert when there was one and out of the corpus
-- when there was not, and only one of the two can ever answer: the outer query reads
-- the snapshot this statement began under, so it cannot see the row the CTE above
-- just wrote. NULL means there is no document, which is the item that carried no
-- reading.

-- document_inserted is the other half of that pair and the two answer different
-- questions. A repeat capture is a fetch that worked and wrote nothing, so a reader
-- counting new material reads this flag while a reader following a document reads the
-- id, and neither has to infer its answer from the other.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  $2::bigint AS domain_id,
  $3::bigint AS source_id,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT n.id FROM written n),
    (SELECT d.id FROM documents d JOIN hashed h ON h.hash = d.hash)) AS document_id,
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM written) AS document_inserted

WITH
-- Where four values become four columns, and the fail and flag halves of
-- fail-flag-keep written as one statement. Judge Source Health decided them and
-- nothing here revisits the decision: the counter, the two stamps and the flag arrive
-- as parameters and are written as they came. src/lib/source-health.ts holds the
-- arithmetic, the node above is where the outcome was read off this pass's readings,
-- and a rule restated down here would be a copy with nothing comparing it against the
-- first.

-- BOTH STAMPS EVERY PASS, including the one that did not move. The answer above holds
-- four values and this statement is built from exactly those, so the stamp being
-- carried through is written back as it came. Writing only the one that moved would
-- mean working out down here which of them did, which is the decision taken a second
-- time in a second language. What the round trip costs is precision and nothing else:
-- the column holds microseconds and the item carried the value as JSON, so a
-- carried-through stamp is rewritten at the millisecond it survived as. Whether a
-- source is broken right now is read off which of the two stamps is the more recent,
-- and a millisecond parts no two passes.

-- Six parameters, in declaration order: the run, the source, the counter, the two
-- stamps and the flag. A stamp the node above could not read as one arrives here as
-- it came and the cast refuses it, loudly, which is the right volume: a NULL written
-- in its place would claim the source has never once succeeded.

-- The write is blind and keyed on the id. The values it applies were worked out from
-- a row read at the top of this pass, so two passes reaching one source at the same
-- time would have the later write win and lose the earlier one's bump. Nothing here
-- locks the row, and what keeps passes apart is a claim taken much further up:
-- ar-dispatch selects a due topic FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and pushes next_run_at
-- forward before it invokes anything, so one topic is in flight once. A domain
-- carrying two topics is what that claim does not cover, and the cost there is a
-- counter short by one rather than a wrong flag, both passes having read the same
-- source and agreed about how it answered.
applied AS (
  UPDATE sources
  -- FOUR COLUMNS AND NO FIFTH. enabled is not in this list and may not be. It is the
  -- operator's column outright, where flagged is the pipeline's own reading, and
  -- src/db/schema/sources.ts keeps the two apart so the rot detector cannot switch
  -- off a feed somebody deliberately turned on. The library answers exactly the four
  -- written here and carries no enabled member for the same reason: a column named in
  -- an answer is a column somebody eventually writes.

  -- flagged is set here and never cleared here, which is a property of the value
  -- rather than of this clause. The library sets it once the counter reaches the
  -- threshold and has no member that unsets it, so this statement can write false
  -- only for a source that was already false. Clearing a flag is an operator's act,
  -- taken once whatever broke has been fixed.
  SET
    consecutive_failures = $3::integer,
    last_success_at = $4::timestamptz,
    last_failure_at = $5::timestamptz,
    flagged = $6::boolean
  WHERE id = $2::bigint
  RETURNING consecutive_failures, flagged
)

SELECT
-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever happened. The update sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT names
-- no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was handed. An
-- UPDATE ... RETURNING on its own emits nothing when its WHERE matches nothing, and
-- the source would then drop out of the stream at the one point where its absence is
-- worth reporting.

-- health_applied is that case named. False means the row this pass read at the top is
-- no longer there, which is a source deleted mid pass rather than a source that
-- failed, and counting the two as one thing is how a deletion turns into a flag
-- nobody can explain.

-- The counter and the flag are read back out of the update rather than echoed from
-- the parameters, so what this node answers is what the row now holds. Nothing else
-- is restated: the readings, their warnings, the config faults and the HTTP status
-- stay on Extract Records' items, where a node below reaches them by name.

-- A pass that succeeded is a counter of 0, and no separate member says so. The
-- library resets to a real zero on a success and to nothing else, and the threshold
-- it compares against is a positive integer, so the two readings are one reading. A
-- member saying it again would be a copy able to disagree with the column beside it.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  $2::bigint AS source_id,
  (SELECT a.consecutive_failures FROM applied a) AS consecutive_failures,
  (SELECT a.flagged FROM applied a) AS flagged,
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM applied) AS health_applied

WITH
-- Where the corpus a new document is held against is read, and the only node in this
-- group that touches the database. The two Code nodes below it cannot: a spliced
-- library imports nothing and a Code node opens no connection, so the corpus arrives
-- here as data or the dedupe below has nothing to hold anything against.

-- ONE READ FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, so it runs against the
-- first item it was handed and answers once. What it selects is a fact about the
-- domain rather than about a source, and Apply Source Health above answers one item
-- per source, so without the setting this statement would run once per source and
-- hand the node below the same corpus over again for each of them. Nothing downstream
-- reads past the first item either way: Mark Near Duplicates takes the first and
-- nothing else, so the setting costs round trips rather than meaning.

-- Two parameters, in declaration order: the run and the domain. The domain is read
-- back off Load Domain Context by name rather than off the item this node was handed,
-- Apply Source Health's projection carrying a source and no domain. The run travels
-- for the reason it travels everywhere on this canvas: a ledger row and the closing
-- update are charged to it and not to a source.
recent AS (
  -- The window, and it is a ROW CAP rather than a span of time. What a dedupe needs
  -- is enough recent material to recognise a repeat in, and how much material that is
  -- depends on how fast a domain moves: a span of days gives a quiet domain almost
  -- nothing to compare against and a busy one more than a pass can sketch. A cap on
  -- rows gives both the same window and lets the domain decide how long it reaches
  -- back.

  -- What the cap costs is said rather than hidden. An item near enough to a document
  -- older than the two hundredth most recent one is not recognised here, and the
  -- exact key in Write Documents is what still catches it when the bytes agree. Two
  -- hundred is a bound on the sketching this pass does rather than a claim about how
  -- long a repeat stays interesting.

  -- Every document of the domain, and neither exclusion a reader expects is made. The
  -- rows this pass just wrote are in the window because they are in the corpus, and
  -- the node below parts a document from itself by id rather than by when a row
  -- arrived. A document whose reading its contract refused is in it too: its body is
  -- content that was captured, and content arriving twice is what this window is for
  -- whatever a contract made of it.
  SELECT d.id, d.body
  FROM documents d
  WHERE d.domain_id = $2::bigint
  ORDER BY d.id DESC
  LIMIT 200
)

SELECT
-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever the domain holds. The corpus is a scalar subquery COALESCEd
-- to an empty array and the outer SELECT names no FROM, so this node answers exactly
-- one item however few documents there are to put in it. A domain with nothing in the
-- corpus yet answers an empty array, which the node below reads as nothing to compare
-- against rather than as a node that did not run.

-- A NULL domain_id selects nothing and reaches the same empty array. That is a pass
-- started by hand rather than by the dispatcher, and Load Domain Context is where the
-- two are told apart.

-- The array is ordered ASCENDING by id while the window above takes the newest rows
-- descending, and the two orders are doing different jobs. The window is about which
-- documents to carry; the order is about which of several converging members a
-- document is marked against, and the node below stops at the first it converges
-- with. Ascending makes that the earliest, which is the row a person following a
-- duplicate back wants to land on.

-- Two members per entry and no more. The id is what orders a pair and what a mark
-- names, the body is what a sketch is built from, and everything else about a
-- document is a question for the table. A hash is deliberately not here: exact
-- repetition was settled in Write Documents, and this window exists for the pairs
-- that key cannot see.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  $2::bigint AS domain_id,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', r.id, 'body', r.body)
       ORDER BY r.id)
       FROM recent r),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS corpus

WITH
-- Where the address of the model this pass calls is read, and the only node in this
-- group that can read it. A Code node opens no connection and a spliced library
-- imports nothing, so the endpoint and the model name arrive here as data or the
-- nodes below have nothing to call.

-- ONE READ FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, so it runs against the
-- first item it was handed and answers once. Gate Documents above answers one item
-- per new document, and which service this deployment calls is a fact about the
-- deployment rather than about a document, so without the setting this statement
-- would run once per document and hand the same row down again for each of them.

-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever the table holds. Every member below is a scalar subquery and
-- the outer SELECT names no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item however few
-- connectors are configured. A deployment with no llm row at all answers one item
-- carrying a null endpoint, which the node below reads as a service that cannot be
-- reached rather than as a node that did not run.

-- A pass with nothing gated in never reaches this node at all, executeOnce having no
-- first item to run against. That is the ordinary quiet pass: no connector is read,
-- no chunk is prepared and no call is made.

-- One parameter, the run, read off the item this node was handed. It travels for the
-- reason it travels everywhere on this canvas: the ledger row below is charged to the
-- run and not to a document.
connector AS (
  -- The llm connector, by kind. connectors is not domain scoped: which model endpoint
  -- answers is a fact about the deployment rather than about any one domain, so there
  -- is no domain to narrow this by and nothing on a domain row names one.

  -- Ordered by id and capped at one, which is a decision rather than a formality. The
  -- natural key is the kind and the name together, so a deployment may configure two
  -- llm connectors and nothing stored anywhere says which of them this pass wants.
  -- The oldest wins, and a deployment moving to a second endpoint reconfigures the
  -- row it has rather than adding a rival to it. Naming one per domain would be a
  -- column on domains and an operator decision, not a read of a key nobody declared.
  SELECT c.id, c.name, c.config
  FROM connectors c
  WHERE c.kind = 'llm'
  ORDER BY c.id
  LIMIT 1
)

SELECT
-- Two members read out of the config object, and both are read the way Write
-- Documents reads the members of a reading: a value that is not a string is not text
-- whatever it would coerce to, and the empty string is an absence rather than a
-- value. connectors.config carries no type annotation, its shape being the client
-- business and different for each kind, so nothing has validated either of these and
-- this projection is where they are first read as text.

-- A null endpoint means there is nowhere to reach. The node below refuses on it by
-- name, which is the last place a pass can stop before a call is attempted against an
-- address nobody configured.

-- A null model is an ordinary state and not a refusal. A gateway that routes, or a
-- runtime serving whatever it was started with, takes no model name, and
-- llm_calls.model is nullable for exactly that: the row still counts as a call while
-- saying nothing about which model made it.

-- connector_id and connector_name are carried for a reader rather than for a caller.
-- Nothing below binds either one, and a total over the ledger that wants to know
-- which service answered has the model name and this pass execution to go on. They
-- travel because the node that made a call and the row that named the service should
-- be readable together on the canvas.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  (SELECT c.id FROM connector c) AS connector_id,
  (SELECT c.name FROM connector c) AS connector_name,
  (SELECT nullif(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(c.config -> 'endpoint') = 'string'
                      THEN c.config ->> 'endpoint'
                 END, '')
     FROM connector c) AS endpoint,
  (SELECT nullif(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(c.config -> 'model') = 'string'
                      THEN c.config ->> 'model'
                 END, '')
     FROM connector c) AS model

WITH
-- Where a call is accounted for. One row per call, charged to the run that made it,
-- and src/db/schema/runs.ts argues at length what that buys: the runs row accounts
-- for a pass as a whole, and these rows account for the same work one call at a time,
-- which is the granularity the question of what a call cost is asked at.

-- THE ATTRIBUTION IS THE POINT. run_id is what charges a call to a pass, and it is
-- the column the design this port draws from declared and never filled: its ledger
-- inserts named the item a call was about, or named nothing at all, so the spend
-- could be summed and no pass could be held to any of it. A total without it says
-- that something is burning and not which step, which schedule or which batch.

-- THE CEILING AND THIS ROW ARE ONE PROPERTY read from two ends. Apply Call Ceiling
-- states what a pass WILL do, and these rows are what it did, so a ceiling that
-- quietly stopped being applied reads exactly like a pass whose input happened to be
-- small. Neither half is enforced by anything in this schema: a call whose row was
-- never written is missing from every total at once and no constraint can notice,
-- which is why the property is asserted over the built artifact instead.

-- ONE ROW OUT PER CALL. The insert sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT names no FROM,
-- so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was handed, and the group
-- below reads a document that was called about whether or not the call came back with
-- anything. An INSERT ... RETURNING on its own would emit nothing for a statement
-- that wrote no row.

-- THREE PARAMETERS, in declaration order: the run, the model name, and the prepared
-- item this call was made from. The first two are read off Select Model Connector,
-- which answered one row for the whole pass, so neither is a per call reading and
-- neither needs pairing.

-- THE THIRD IS BOUND BY POSITION, and this is the one pairing on this canvas that is
-- not a name or an id. Extract Finding Fields replaced the item that carried the
-- measurements, the way every node in the middle of this chain replaces what it was
-- handed, and it answers one item per item it ran on, so the item at this position in
-- its output was made from the item at the same position in Prepare Model Prompt. The
-- paired item form would read the same members through the links a node records,
-- which depends on that node recording them; the position depends on the cardinality,
-- which the setting on that node fixes.

-- What being wrong about it would cost is small and worth saying rather than leaving
-- to be discovered: two calls in the same pass would swap their sizes. The run total,
-- which is what this ledger is read for, is exact either way. The ids are the members
-- where a swap would matter, and they are read out of the same object, so a
-- mis-pairing files the whole row under the wrong document rather than half of it.

-- BOUND AS ONE JSONB VALUE rather than as a member per column. Fewer values for the
-- comma splitter to get wrong, and the members are read out here where a comment can
-- say what each one is, instead of in an expression no gate reads.
prepared AS (
  SELECT $3::jsonb AS item
),

-- What the row says about the call, cast once. prompt_chars and est_tokens are in the
-- signal class the schema calls out: null means nothing measured this call, and zero
-- is a real reading rather than a stand in for one, a call declined before it was
-- sent having sent no characters. Neither is COALESCEd to zero for exactly that
-- reason.

-- The node name is a literal, and known by construction rather than looked up: the
-- step that made the call is the node above this one and its own name is the one fact
-- it cannot fail to have. It moves if that node is renamed, and every row already
-- written keeps the old name, which is a fact about totals over a long window that
-- nothing in the schema can hold together.

-- The model is nullable and arrives so. A gateway that routes, or a runtime serving
-- whatever it was started with, takes no model name, and what is stored here is what
-- was asked for rather than what served it.
call AS (
  SELECT
    nullif($2::text, '') AS model,
    (p.item ->> 'prompt_chars')::integer AS prompt_chars,
    (p.item ->> 'est_tokens')::integer AS est_tokens
  FROM prepared p
),

-- The write. No conflict target and no ON CONFLICT clause: a ledger has no key to
-- collide on, every call being its own event, and two calls made about one document
-- in two passes are two rows on purpose.
written AS (
  INSERT INTO llm_calls (run_id, node, model, prompt_chars, est_tokens)
  SELECT
    $1::bigint,
    'Extract Finding Fields',
    c.model,
    c.prompt_chars,
    c.est_tokens
  FROM call c
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and it is about the document rather than about the
-- call. The three ids come back out of the prepared item so the group below has the
-- row a finding is written against, and the answer the model gave is deliberately not
-- among them: it is untrusted text, it is reachable off Extract Finding Fields by
-- name, and routing it through a SQL parameter to get it here would be a round trip
-- that changes nothing about it.

-- llm_call_id is the ledger row this call left behind. Nothing below reads it today.
-- It travels because the row and the item it was written for are otherwise joined by
-- nothing at all, this table carrying no reference to a document.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  (SELECT (p.item ->> 'domain_id')::bigint FROM prepared p) AS domain_id,
  (SELECT (p.item ->> 'source_id')::bigint FROM prepared p) AS source_id,
  (SELECT (p.item ->> 'document_id')::bigint FROM prepared p) AS document_id,
  (SELECT w.id FROM written w) AS llm_call_id

WITH
-- Where a validated answer becomes a row, and the last write this pass makes about a
-- document. The core columns are neutral and mean the same thing in every domain, and
-- everything this one needed beyond them is the fields payload the node above checked
-- against its contract. findings in src/db/schema/findings.ts argues that split at
-- length: it is what lets one table serve every domain, and neither half works alone.

-- A REWRITE AND NOT A RENAME. The design this port draws from wrote its results into
-- a table whose columns were its subject matter, one column per thing that subject
-- happened to have, so a second subject was a migration and a query per subject.
-- Nothing of that shape survives here. What a domain needs beyond the neutral columns
-- is a key in the JSONB payload the domain itself declares, which is why this
-- statement names a domain, a document and a payload, and names nothing that could
-- belong to one subject alone.

-- WHAT A REFUSED ANSWER DOES HERE is nothing, which is the point. The WHERE clause is
-- the whole of it: an item whose payload is absent inserts no row, the outer SELECT
-- still answers, and the document goes on standing exactly as it did with no finding
-- hung off it. Raising instead would lose the findings every other document in this
-- batch produced, over one model's reply about one of them.

-- ONE ROW OUT PER ITEM. The insert sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT reads the one
-- row the parameter made, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was
-- handed whether or not it wrote anything. An INSERT ... RETURNING on its own would
-- emit nothing for a refused answer, and the item would vanish from the stream at
-- exactly the point where a refusal is an ordinary outcome.

-- ONE PARAMETER, the item itself. Fewer values for the comma splitter to get wrong
-- than a member per column, and the members are read out below where a comment can
-- say what each one is instead of inside an expression no gate reads.
item AS (
  SELECT $1::jsonb AS payload
),

-- The members, cast once. The ids arrive as the node above carried them and are not
-- re-derived here, which is the rule every node on this canvas follows: a value
-- copied forward can be wrong, and a value computed twice can disagree with itself.

-- fields is the payload the node above validated, or SQL NULL where it refused.
-- jsonb_typeof is what parts the two: an absent member and a JSON null both answer
-- something other than object, so both come through as NULL and neither reaches the
-- insert. A JavaScript null bound inside a JSONB value is the JSON null literal
-- rather than SQL NULL, which is the trap this reading exists for.

-- document_id is NOT NULL on the table and is not defended here. Every item that
-- reaches this node came through Mark Near Duplicates, which passes on the documents
-- this pass inserted and refuses anything it cannot order, so a null arriving is a
-- canvas contradicting itself rather than an absence to handle. The column reports
-- it, loudly, which is the right volume for a state that cannot happen.
finding AS (
  SELECT
    (i.payload ->> 'run_id')::bigint AS run_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'domain_id')::bigint AS domain_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'source_id')::bigint AS source_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'document_id')::bigint AS document_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'llm_call_id')::bigint AS llm_call_id,
    CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(i.payload -> 'finding_fields') = 'object'
         THEN i.payload -> 'finding_fields'
    END AS fields
  FROM item i
),

-- The write, and the columns it names are the whole of what this pass knows. Every
-- other one is left to the table, each for its own reason.

-- entity_id stays null, and null there is an ordinary state rather than a gap:
-- findings.entity_id says a finding is attributed when the pipeline can name the
-- subject behind it, and plenty are worth keeping without one. Nothing on this canvas
-- resolves an entity, and a placeholder subject to hang the unattributed ones off is
-- the exact shape that column refuses.

-- score and score_version stay null together, which findings.score_version asks for
-- in as many words: the two are written by one statement or by neither, and a score
-- stored with no version survives every re-score the pin exists to trigger. ar-score
-- is the statement that writes them, invoked by the group that closes this pass.

-- created_at takes its default, the insert being when the finding was made.

-- No ON CONFLICT clause, because there is no key to collide on. A document reaches
-- this node once: Mark Near Duplicates passes on the rows this pass INSERTED, so a
-- repeat capture never gets here, and two findings about one document would be two
-- passes over a document only one of them could have inserted.
written AS (
  INSERT INTO findings (domain_id, document_id, fields)
  SELECT f.domain_id, f.document_id, f.fields
  FROM finding f
  WHERE f.fields IS NOT NULL
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, which is about the document rather than about the
-- write. The ids it arrived with travel on because the group that closes this pass is
-- charged to the run and reads its counts off what came through here.

-- finding_id is the row this answer left behind, or null where the answer was
-- refused. That null is the only reading of a refusal any node below has: the
-- sentence saying why sits on the item the node above built and reaches no column,
-- findings having nowhere to put a finding that was not made.

-- llm_call_id travels one node further for the same reason it travelled here. It is
-- the only join between a call that was charged and the finding that call produced,
-- this table carrying no reference to a ledger row and that one carrying no reference
-- to a document.
  f.run_id,
  f.domain_id,
  f.source_id,
  f.document_id,
  f.llm_call_id,
  (SELECT w.id FROM written w) AS finding_id
FROM finding f

WITH
-- Where a vector and the version that dates it become one row, together or not at
-- all. documents.features and documents.feature_version are written by a single
-- statement because the schema asks for exactly that: a vector stored with a null
-- version reads as present to everything looking for one, and there is no version for
-- a recompute to find it stale by, so it survives every pass the pin exists to
-- trigger.

-- ONE PARAMETER, the item itself, which is the shape every write on this canvas uses.
-- Fewer values for the comma splitter to get wrong than a member per column, and the
-- members are read out below where a comment can say what each one is instead of
-- inside an expression no gate reads. The vector is a JSONB object in its own right,
-- so binding the item whole is also the only spelling that keeps it one.

-- ONE ROW OUT PER ITEM. The update sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT reads the row
-- the parameter made, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was
-- handed whether or not the update matched anything. An UPDATE ... RETURNING on its
-- own would emit nothing where it matched nothing, and the item would leave the
-- stream at the point where the write not landing is the thing worth reporting.
item AS (
  SELECT $1::jsonb AS payload
),

-- The members, cast once. The ids arrive as the node above carried them and are not
-- re-derived here, which is the rule every node on this canvas follows.

-- features is the record the node above built, taken only where it is a JSON object.
-- An absent member and a JSON null both answer something else to jsonb_typeof, so
-- both come through as SQL NULL rather than as a vector of nothing: a JavaScript null
-- bound inside a JSONB value is the JSON null literal and not SQL NULL, which is the
-- trap this reading exists for.

-- feature_version_matches_domain is the composed version held against
-- domains.feature_version by the node above. Nothing here acts on it and no column
-- stores it. It rides as far as the outer SELECT so an execution says whether the
-- vectors this pass wrote are at the generation the domain's pin claims, which is a
-- fact about the domain that a capture pass can report and cannot repair.
vector AS (
  SELECT
    (i.payload ->> 'run_id')::bigint AS run_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'domain_id')::bigint AS domain_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'source_id')::bigint AS source_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'document_id')::bigint AS document_id,
    CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(i.payload -> 'features') = 'object'
         THEN i.payload -> 'features'
    END AS features,
    (i.payload ->> 'feature_version')::integer AS feature_version,
    (i.payload ->> 'feature_version_matches_domain')::boolean
      AS feature_version_matches_domain
  FROM item i
),

-- The write, and the pair is the whole of it. Both columns are set or neither is,
-- which is what the WHERE enforces: an item carrying no vector, or no version to pin
-- one with, updates nothing and comes back saying so.

-- Nothing else on the row is touched. The body, the hash, the parse status and the
-- raw payload were all settled by Write Documents several nodes above, and a
-- featurizer rewriting any of them would be answering a question nobody asked it.

-- No ON CONFLICT and no guard against running twice over one document, the id being
-- the key and an UPDATE being idempotent: the same item written a second time stores
-- the same vector under the same version. What nothing here prevents is a DIFFERENT
-- vector arriving for a document already featurized, which is the recompute's subject
-- and is exactly what the version beside it makes visible.
written AS (
  UPDATE documents d
     SET features = v.features,
         feature_version = v.feature_version
    FROM vector v
   WHERE d.id = v.document_id
     AND v.features IS NOT NULL
     AND v.feature_version IS NOT NULL
  RETURNING d.id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, which is about the document rather than about the
-- write. The ids travel because the group that closes this pass is charged to the run
-- and reads its counts off what came through here.

-- document_featurized is whether the update matched a row. False for an item that
-- carried no vector to write, and false is the whole of what a caller learns: the
-- reason a vector is absent sits on the item the node above built and reaches no
-- column, documents having nowhere to put an account of a vector that was not
-- computed.
  v.run_id,
  v.domain_id,
  v.source_id,
  v.document_id,
  v.feature_version,
  v.feature_version_matches_domain,
  (SELECT w.id FROM written w) IS NOT NULL AS document_featurized
FROM vector v

WITH
-- Where a finding becomes an intention to research its subject, and the only row this
-- pass writes that a person has to rule on before anything acts on it. research_pool
-- in src/db/schema/entities.ts is that gate, and its whole argument is that noticing
-- a subject is worth looking into and actually looking are separate events, written
-- by different things at different times. This node is the noticing half. Nothing
-- here searches anything, and nothing here approves anything.

-- WHAT THIS PASS FOUND WORTH RESEARCHING is every finding it wrote that carries a
-- string somebody could search for, and both halves of that sentence are doing work.
-- A finding exists only for a document this pass fetched, hashed, stored, held
-- against the corpus, scored past the free gate and fitted inside the call ceiling,
-- whose answer then came back in the shape its domain asked for. Six filters ran
-- before this statement, so the noticing is already narrow. The one this adds is the
-- last: an intention nobody could turn into a query is not raised at all.
-- research_pool.search_terms records why that matters, an empty list being storable
-- and the drain meeting one closing the row rather than searching for nothing, which
-- is a row an operator ruled on for no reason.

-- THE TERMS ARE THE FINDING'S OWN STRINGS, read back off the payload rather than
-- composed here. findings.fields holds exactly the members
-- DomainSettings.fieldContract declares and exactly the types it declared them at,
-- Validate Finding Fields above having refused any answer whose member was the wrong
-- shape and dropped any member the contract does not name. So jsonb_typeof over the
-- stored payload IS that contract as it was applied. Reading it that way rather than
-- fetching settings.fieldContract again is what keeps this statement from carrying a
-- second copy of a rule able to stop agreeing with the first.

-- EACH TERM IS TRIMMED, DEDUPLICATED, ORDERED, AND DROPPED IF IT IS LONG. Trimming is
-- what makes the deduplication do real work: two spellings of one word differing only
-- in whitespace are one thing to search for and two lines in a listing an operator
-- reads. The bound is 80 characters, which is MAX_ENTITY_NAME_LENGTH in
-- src/lib/validate-entity-name.ts. A value past it is an extraction that has turned
-- into a payload rather than a name, which is that module's own reading of the same
-- number, and that module is the capability gate these strings meet again in phase 6
-- before any of them reaches a request. The number is written out here because a
-- statement can splice nothing; the module is where it is declared and where the
-- argument for it lives.

-- entity_id stays null, and nothing on this canvas resolves one.
-- research_pool.entity_id records that an intention raised from a finding whose
-- subject nothing has attributed is an ordinary row, and that the terms are what
-- makes it researchable anyway. What it refuses is the alternative: one placeholder
-- entity standing for every unnamed subject there is. status takes its pending
-- default, the only state a row nobody has looked at can honestly hold, and
-- approved_at and researched_at are left null, which is where the gate wants them and
-- where research_pool_approval_check holds them.

-- ONE INTENTION PER FINDING, and the NOT EXISTS below is the whole of the
-- deduplication. research_pool carries no unique key and could not be given one over
-- two nullable columns, so deduplicating is the writer's, which that table says in as
-- many words. The reader this guard is written for is ar-score, whose own closing
-- group raises intentions over findings this one may have covered already: a second
-- row for one finding is a second thing to rule on saying nothing new, and an
-- operator who rejected the first would meet it again. It is a read of the snapshot
-- this statement began under, so two passes raising for one finding at the same
-- instant is a race nothing here closes; the cost of losing it is a duplicate in a
-- queue rather than a duplicate search.

-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever was raised. The insert sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT
-- names no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item however many rows it wrote,
-- including none. Both nodes below are built on that. The item is the hand-over Score
-- Findings gives ar-score, and Close Run needs exactly one execution to write exactly
-- one row.

-- RUNS ONCE FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, so it runs against the
-- first item it was handed and reads the findings off Write Findings by name. Those
-- are different populations: the stream arriving here is one item per document
-- featurized, and a statement mapped over it would raise this pass's intentions once
-- per document. No gate in this repository reads a node-level property, so nothing
-- reports that setting going missing except a duplicate this statement's own NOT
-- EXISTS then turns away.

-- AN ID IS TESTED AS TEXT AND NEVER BY TYPE, which is the one reading on this canvas
-- that cannot be taken on trust. A bigint read as a top-level column comes back off
-- the driver as a STRING, so Write Findings answers a finding_id spelled "41", while
-- an id that was inside a jsonb_agg array was parsed out of JSON and arrives as the
-- number 41. Both spellings reach this statement from different nodes of one
-- workflow, so jsonb_typeof answers number for some ids and string for others, and a
-- predicate written on the type silently drops half of them: measured, a type test
-- over Write Findings' own projection matched nothing at all and this node raised no
-- intention for a pass that wrote seven findings. The regex below reads the TEXT of
-- the member, which is the same for both spellings and is NULL for an absent member
-- and for a JSON null, so one predicate covers a refused answer, a projection that
-- stopped carrying the member, and anything that is not an id at all.

-- TWO PARAMETERS AND A THIRD, in declaration order: the findings this pass wrote as
-- one jsonb array, the run, and the domain. The findings travel as one value rather
-- than one per member because the comma splitter has fewer things to get wrong that
-- way, and because the array is what a jsonb function reads. The run and the domain
-- are read off Load Domain Context rather than off the stream, every Postgres node
-- between having replaced the item several times over.

-- The findings, as Write Findings answered them. That node emits one item per item it
-- was handed whether or not it wrote a row, so an item carrying a null finding_id is
-- a model answer the contract refused, and it is filtered below rather than defended
-- against here.
item AS (
  SELECT $1::jsonb AS payload
),

-- The ids, read as text for the reason the header gives. A refused answer carries a
-- null finding_id, an absent member reads the same way, and neither matches, so one
-- predicate covers both and covers a member holding something that is not an id at
-- all. DISTINCT because these ids are what the outer SELECT hands ar-score, and a
-- repeated one there would ask for a finding to be scored twice.
finding AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT (w.value ->> 'finding_id')::bigint AS finding_id
  FROM item i,
       jsonb_array_elements(
         CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(i.payload) = 'array'
              THEN i.payload
              ELSE '[]'::jsonb
         END) AS w(value)
  WHERE (w.value ->> 'finding_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
),

-- The rows themselves, read back rather than carried. Write Findings answered ids and
-- nothing else, and what the terms are read out of is the payload as it was stored,
-- so this join is what puts the two together. domain_id comes off the finding rather
-- than off the parameter: an intention is filed under the domain of the finding that
-- raised it, which is the same domain the pass ran for and is read from the row that
-- is actually being cited.

-- The terms. A member the contract declared as anything other than a string has no
-- spelling a search could be issued with, and a member the answer never stated is not
-- in the payload at all, so one type test covers both. The CASE around the payload is
-- not defensive dressing: jsonb_each raises on a value that is not an object,
-- findings.fields is NOT NULL with a {} default and can hold any JSON a writer put
-- there, and a raise here would leave the run open at the node whose job is closing
-- it.

-- The empty list is what a finding with nothing searchable comes to, and it is the
-- value the insert filters on rather than a row anybody stores.
subject AS (
  SELECT
    f.id,
    f.domain_id,
    COALESCE(
      (SELECT jsonb_agg(DISTINCT t.term ORDER BY t.term)
         FROM (
           SELECT btrim(e.value #>> '{}') AS term
             FROM jsonb_each(
                    CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(f.fields) = 'object'
                         THEN f.fields
                         ELSE '{}'::jsonb
                    END) e
            WHERE jsonb_typeof(e.value) = 'string') t
        WHERE t.term <> ''
          AND length(t.term) <= 80),
      '[]'::jsonb) AS search_terms
  FROM findings f
  JOIN finding n ON n.finding_id = f.id
),

-- The write, and the two predicates are the whole of what it decides. A finding
-- yielding no term raises nothing, and a finding already carrying an intention raises
-- nothing.

-- No ON CONFLICT clause, because there is no key to collide on: research_pool has
-- none and cannot be given one over two nullable columns. The NOT EXISTS above is
-- what stands in its place, and the difference between the two is worth knowing
-- rather than glossing. A unique key refuses at the instant of the write; this reads
-- a snapshot and can be beaten by a concurrent pass.
raised AS (
  INSERT INTO research_pool (domain_id, finding_id, search_terms)
  SELECT s.domain_id, s.id, s.search_terms
  FROM subject s
  WHERE jsonb_array_length(s.search_terms) > 0
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM research_pool p
      WHERE p.finding_id = s.id)
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and it is the hand-over as much as the report. Score
-- Findings below passes it to ar-score whole, so every member here is either what
-- that workflow needs or what Close Run reads back by name.

-- ingest_run_id names what it is. It is this pass's run and it is provenance, not a
-- run ar-score may write to: ar-score closes a runs row of its own, and a member
-- spelled run_id would be read by the first node of a workflow written to the shape
-- this one is written to, which resolves its domain out of exactly that member. The
-- name is the whole of what keeps the two apart, since nothing in the schema does.

-- domain_id is what ar-score fetches its own criteria, terms and personas against. It
-- is the pass's domain rather than any finding's, and it is NULL for a run id that
-- resolved to nothing, which is the discriminator Load Domain Context puts on every
-- item.

-- finding_ids is every finding this pass wrote, which is not the same list as the
-- intentions below: a finding whose fields hold nothing searchable is scored like any
-- other. Ordered so two passes over one unchanged domain hand ar-score the same list
-- in the same order.

-- intention_ids is what was raised, and it is a list rather than a count so that
-- Close Run tallies it the way it tallies every other node's items, through one
-- reading rather than through a special case.
  $2::bigint AS ingest_run_id,
  $3::bigint AS domain_id,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(n.finding_id ORDER BY n.finding_id) FROM finding n),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS finding_ids,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(r.id ORDER BY r.id) FROM raised r),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS intention_ids

WITH
-- Where the pass says what it did and stops being open. runs in src/db/schema/runs.ts
-- keeps that account in three columns because a reader wanting any one of them should
-- not have to parse the other two: status is what the pass came to, counts is what it
-- did, and errors is what it could not do. This statement writes all three and the
-- finish beside them.

-- STATUS AND finished_at ARE SET TOGETHER because nothing in the schema holds them
-- together. A row saying failed with no finish, or carrying a finish while still
-- saying running, is storable, and runs.status records that only the writer pairs
-- them. Close Run Failed in ar-dispatch is that writer for the rows the dispatcher
-- closes, and this is it for the row a pass closes about itself.

-- THE DISPATCHER WRITES THIS ROW AFTER THIS NODE DOES, and the overlap is real rather
-- than theoretical. ar-dispatch opened this run, waits for this workflow, and then
-- sets status and finished_at itself, so an ok from there lands on top of a partial
-- written here. Its own Close Run Succeeded predicted the case and left the choice to
-- this phase, between reading errors on that side and holding every target to
-- reporting its own status. What survives either way is counts, which no statement in
-- ar-dispatch touches, and errors, which both sides APPEND to rather than assign. So
-- the status this node writes is the pass's own reading of itself, and the row's last
-- word on it belongs to whoever wrote last.

-- THE TALLIES ARE COUNTED HERE AND GATHERED THERE. The parameter below carries one
-- array per node, each cut to the members a tally reads, and every rule about what
-- those members MEAN is in this statement: what counts as a source that failed, as a
-- document that was already there, as an answer the contract turned away. An
-- expression can import nothing and is read by no gate in this repository, so a rule
-- written there would be a second copy of something with nowhere to be compared.
-- Naming and projection are what the expression does, and the projection is not
-- cosmetic: the items it reads carry whole payloads and whole document bodies, and
-- binding them unprojected would ship the pass's corpus back to the database to be
-- counted.

-- AN ID IS TESTED AS TEXT AND NEVER BY TYPE, and the two spellings reaching this node
-- come from one workflow. A bigint read as a top-level column comes back off the
-- driver as a STRING, so Write Documents answers a document_id spelled "41" and Write
-- Findings a finding_id spelled the same way, while duplicate_of was parsed out of a
-- jsonb_agg array by Mark Near Duplicates and arrives as the number 41. A tally
-- written on jsonb_typeof would count one of those and miss the other, which is a
-- count that is wrong by a plausible amount rather than one that fails. Every id
-- predicate below reads the member's TEXT, which is the same either way and is NULL
-- for an absent member and for a JSON null.

-- EVERY LIST IS NORMALISED ONCE. The reading CTE below turns the gathered object into
-- one row per item with the node it came from beside it, so a tally is a count over
-- that with a predicate, and a member that arrived as something other than an array
-- contributes nothing instead of raising. The raise is the failure worth designing
-- against here rather than anywhere else on this canvas: this is the node that closes
-- the run, and a statement that threw would leave the row open with everything it is
-- reporting on already done.

-- WHAT MAKES A PASS PARTIAL is a source that failed, and an invocation that did not
-- complete, of the two this canvas makes. RUN_STATUSES in src/db/schema/values.ts
-- argues that member at length as the one fail-flag-keep needs: a pass that read six
-- sources and lost one produced real work and a real failure at once, and both
-- neighbours lose half of it. failed is the narrower case where every source read
-- failed, so there is no half to keep. A pass that read no source at all is ok rather
-- than failed, that being a domain with nothing switched on rather than a domain that
-- stopped working. Neither invocation moves it past partial: a scoring pass and a
-- research pass are both work this pass asked another workflow for, and a failure to
-- reach one says nothing about the documents this one read and stored.

-- WHAT DOES NOT MAKE IT PARTIAL is a refused model answer, and that is a decision
-- rather than an oversight. The sticky note over the finding group says why in full:
-- the document was fetched, hashed, stored, compared and gated before a call was
-- made, each of those left a row, and a reply in the wrong shape says nothing about
-- any of them. It is counted, under answers_refused, and counting it is what a tally
-- is for.

-- THE ERRORS ENTRIES ARE ONE PER FAILURE and are APPENDED. runs.errors defaults to an
-- empty list and is one entry per failure, and this row's id is the item ar-dispatch
-- forwarded, so entries may be here already; assigning a fresh list would drop
-- somebody else's account of the same run. A source that failed gets an entry naming
-- it, which is what makes partial legible to the digest that reads this column rather
-- than a status nobody can explain. A refused answer gets none, for the reason above.

-- RUNS ONCE FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, so it writes one row
-- however many items Score Findings above answered with, that count being whatever
-- ar-score returned rather than anything this canvas fixes. Without it a scoring pass
-- answering three items would close this run three times, which costs nothing but
-- says the wrong thing about how many passes there were.

-- WHAT REACHES THIS NODE, and it is the honest limit of the whole group. Every node
-- on this canvas is on one main chain, and a node handed no item does not run, so a
-- pass that selected no source, or whose gate ignored every document, or whose
-- ceiling admitted none, stops before here and leaves its runs row at the running
-- default. ar-dispatch cannot finish it either, its success branch having no item to
-- fire on when this workflow returns none. That is one shape and it wants one repair,
-- a branch off Load Domain Context that closes a run nothing else reached, and this
-- group does not add it: the closing group is where the cost shows and the topology
-- is where the fix goes.

-- FOUR PARAMETERS, in declaration order: the run, the gathered pass, and the two
-- errors an invoking node kept in the stream when the workflow it called did not
-- complete, Score Findings first and Research Candidates second. The run is read off
-- Load Domain Context by name rather than off the item, which is where it survives a
-- domain that resolved to nothing. Each error is stringified on the way in for the
-- reason Close Run Failed in ar-dispatch stringifies its own: a parameter is split on
-- commas unless it parses as JSON on its own, and an executor's message routinely
-- carries one.

gathered AS (
  SELECT
    $1::bigint AS run_id,
    CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof($2::jsonb) = 'object'
         THEN $2::jsonb
         ELSE '{}'::jsonb
    END AS pass,
    nullif($3::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS score_error,
    nullif($4::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS research_error
),

-- The gathered pass, one row per item with the node it came from beside it.
-- jsonb_each raises on a value that is not an object and jsonb_array_elements on one
-- that is not an array, so both are guarded rather than trusted, and a member that
-- arrived as neither is simply absent from every tally below.
reading AS (
  SELECT e.key AS node, x.item AS item
  FROM gathered g,
       jsonb_each(g.pass) e,
       jsonb_array_elements(
         CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(e.value) = 'array'
              THEN e.value
              ELSE '[]'::jsonb
         END) AS x(item)
),

-- What the pass did, one count per question a reader of a digest asks. Every one of
-- them is a count over the reading above with a predicate, and the predicates are the
-- part worth reading: each is written against the shape its node actually answers
-- rather than against a cast that could raise on something else.

-- A boolean is compared as jsonb rather than cast to one, an id is matched as text,
-- and a counter is matched as text before it is cast. Between them that is why no
-- tally here can stop the run being closed.

-- documents_ignored is the gate's only durable record. Gate Documents scores every
-- new document against the domain's terms and nothing stores the decision it reaches,
-- so this count is the whole of what survives the execution about work that was
-- deliberately not done. duplicates_marked sits beside it for the same reason.
tally AS (
  SELECT
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'sources') AS sources_read,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'health'
        AND (item ->> 'consecutive_failures') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
        AND (item ->> 'consecutive_failures')::integer > 0) AS sources_failed,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'health'
        AND item -> 'flagged' = 'true'::jsonb) AS sources_flagged,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'records'
        AND item = '"failed"'::jsonb) AS records_refused,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'documents'
        AND item -> 'document_inserted' = 'true'::jsonb) AS documents_written,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'documents'
        AND (item ->> 'document_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
        AND item -> 'document_inserted' = 'false'::jsonb) AS documents_repeated,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'duplicates'
        AND (item #>> '{}') ~ '^[0-9]+$') AS duplicates_marked,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'gates'
        AND item = '"ignore"'::jsonb) AS documents_ignored,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'calls'
        AND (item #>> '{}') ~ '^[0-9]+$') AS model_calls,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'answers'
        AND jsonb_typeof(item) = 'string') AS answers_refused,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'findings'
        AND (item #>> '{}') ~ '^[0-9]+$') AS findings_written,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'vectors'
        AND item = 'true'::jsonb) AS documents_featurized,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'intentions') AS intentions_raised
),

-- What the pass could not do, one entry per failure, in the shape Close Run Failed in
-- ar-dispatch already writes: the node that met it and the values that say what it
-- was. A source entry names the row and the counters the health group left on it, so
-- the digest that reads this column can say which feed stopped working rather than
-- only that something did.

-- The ordinal is what keeps two passes over one unchanged run reporting in the same
-- order. It orders the two KINDS of entry; the entries within a kind are ordered by
-- their own text, the health items arriving in whatever order the stream held them.
failure AS (
  SELECT
    1 AS ordinal,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'node', 'Apply Source Health',
      'source_id', r.item -> 'source_id',
      'consecutive_failures', r.item -> 'consecutive_failures',
      'flagged', r.item -> 'flagged') AS entry
  FROM reading r
  WHERE r.node = 'health'
    AND (r.item ->> 'consecutive_failures') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
    AND (r.item ->> 'consecutive_failures')::integer > 0

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    2 AS ordinal,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'node', 'Score Findings',
      'error', g.score_error) AS entry
  FROM gathered g
  WHERE g.score_error IS NOT NULL

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    3 AS ordinal,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'node', 'Research Candidates',
      'error', g.research_error) AS entry
  FROM gathered g
  WHERE g.research_error IS NOT NULL
),

-- The three things the update writes, worked out before it runs so that the statement
-- below is a write and not a decision.
outcome AS (
  SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN t.sources_read > 0 AND t.sources_failed = t.sources_read
        THEN 'failed'
      WHEN t.sources_failed > 0
        OR g.score_error IS NOT NULL
        OR g.research_error IS NOT NULL
        THEN 'partial'
      ELSE 'ok'
    END AS status,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'sources_read', t.sources_read,
      'sources_failed', t.sources_failed,
      'sources_flagged', t.sources_flagged,
      'records_refused', t.records_refused,
      'documents_written', t.documents_written,
      'documents_repeated', t.documents_repeated,
      'duplicates_marked', t.duplicates_marked,
      'documents_ignored', t.documents_ignored,
      'model_calls', t.model_calls,
      'answers_refused', t.answers_refused,
      'findings_written', t.findings_written,
      'documents_featurized', t.documents_featurized,
      'intentions_raised', t.intentions_raised) AS counts,
    COALESCE(
      (SELECT jsonb_agg(f.entry ORDER BY f.ordinal, f.entry) FROM failure f),
      '[]'::jsonb) AS entries
  FROM gathered g, tally t
),

-- The write. One row, matched on the run this pass was started with, and nothing else
-- on it is touched: domain_id, started_at and scheduled_by were settled when
-- ar-dispatch opened it, and a closing statement rewriting any of them would be
-- answering a question nobody asked it.

-- No guard against running twice. Closing a run is idempotent in everything but the
-- finish and the appended entries: a second pass over one run would write the same
-- counts and the same status, move finished_at, and append the same failures again.
-- Nothing on this canvas can produce that second pass, executeOnce leaving exactly
-- one execution and the chain above reaching this node once.
closed AS (
  UPDATE runs r
     SET status = o.status,
         finished_at = now(),
         counts = o.counts,
         errors = r.errors || o.entries
    FROM gathered g, outcome o
   WHERE r.id = g.run_id
  RETURNING r.id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and the last one this workflow emits. It is what
-- ar-dispatch's Invoke Target Workflow hands to its own closing statement, and the
-- whole reason this node answers exactly one: that branch runs once per item it
-- receives, so a group answering per document would close the dispatcher's row once
-- per document.

-- run_closed is whether the update matched a row. False means the run this pass was
-- started with is no longer there, which is a row deleted mid pass rather than a pass
-- that failed, and the two are worth telling apart in an execution nobody is
-- watching.

-- counts and status travel because they are what this node decided, and reading them
-- back off the answer is cheaper than reading the row again.
  g.run_id,
  o.status,
  o.counts,
  jsonb_array_length(o.entries) AS errors_appended,
  (SELECT c.id FROM closed c) IS NOT NULL AS run_closed
FROM gathered g, outcome o
