## Invoked, Never Scheduled

This workflow starts when `ar-dispatch` reaches it through Invoke Target Workflow, and the Execute Workflow Trigger on this canvas is the whole of what makes that possible. It holds no clock and may not acquire one: `ar-dispatch` carries the only Schedule Trigger in the system, and `tests/invariants/workflows.test.ts` counts them across every built workflow and names the one file allowed to hold one.

Scheduling this workflow is a row instead. A `topics` row says how often a domain should be pulled and when it is next due, the dispatcher claims it once `next_run_at` has passed, and this workflow is invoked for the claim. So changing the cadence is an UPDATE rather than an edit to this canvas.

### What arrives, and what does not

One item carrying `run_id`, and nothing else. `Open Run` opens the `runs` row before the invocation and its `RETURNING` projection is the item forwarded here, so the claimed topic does not survive the hop: what this workflow knows about the pass it is running is the run, and the domain is read back off that. `Load Domain Context` is where that happens.

The trigger is typeVersion 1, which passes the caller's item through as it stands. Nothing here declares an input schema, so what the dispatcher sends is what the first node reads, and adding a schema later is a change to both ends rather than to this node alone.

### Started by hand

A run started from this canvas rather than by the dispatcher carries no `run_id`, and nothing pretends otherwise. `Load Domain Context` answers a null `domain_id` and four empty lists, which is a shape a node below can refuse by name. It is not an error worth suppressing: a pass with no run to charge has nowhere to write what it did.

## Flagged Is Not Disabled

Two columns keep a source out of this pass, and they are not one column written twice. `Select Active Sources` reads both: `enabled AND NOT flagged`.

`flagged` is the pipeline's own reading, and the flag half of fail-flag-keep. `src/lib/source-health.ts` decides it: handed a source's counters and one fetch outcome, it answers a `flagged` of true once `consecutive_failures` has reached the threshold. Skipping the row is what makes setting the flag worth anything. A rotted feed that goes on being fetched spends a request every pass, stores payloads nothing can read, and buries the sources still worth reading underneath them.

Nothing on this canvas clears it. `source-health.ts` sets the flag and has no member that unsets it, and `Apply Source Health` writes back exactly what it was answered, so a `false` reaches the column only for a source whose flag was already false. A flag the same automation could clear is a source that alternates quietly between working and not with nobody told, and the repair is usually a new `parser_config`, which is a pending row and an approval of its own. Clearing it is an operator's act, taken once what broke has been fixed.

### Switching a source off is a column of its own

`enabled` is the operator's outright, and the two are separate because they answer different questions. `flagged` says the pipeline believes this feed has stopped working; `enabled` says whether it may be read at all. Collapsing them would let the detector switch off a feed an operator deliberately turned on, and leave nowhere to record a suspect source still worth reading.

### What a skipped source costs

Nothing on this pass and nothing after it. A source this node does not select produces no item, so nothing is requested for it, no document is written under it, and its counter and its two stamps stay where the last pass left them. Which sources a domain is skipping is a question for the table, and the rows are the answer.

A domain whose sources are all switched off or flagged selects nothing at all, and the chain below is skipped whole. The `runs` row still closes: `ar-dispatch` opened it and waits for this workflow to return, so a pass with nothing to fetch ends looking like the pass it was.

## One Request Per Source

`Fetch Source Payload` runs once for every item `Select Active Sources` answered, so that statement's row count is this pass's request count and nothing here loops. A source is reached once per pass, and paging across passes is what the cursor is for.

### The cursor travels as a query parameter

`sources.cursor` is opaque text: only the adapter that wrote it has to understand it, and this node does not read it at all. It is sent under whatever name `parser_config.cursor_param` gives, and a source naming none sends no cursor. There is no default name, because guessing one puts a parameter nobody asked for on every request, where a source ignoring it looks exactly like a source honouring it.

A NULL cursor sends nothing either. The column stores an absence rather than an empty string, and an empty string handed back to a source is a real position.

What that does not serve is a cursor an API takes as a header, an entity tag being the usual one. `src/sources/paged-list.ts` sends those Node side, over an endpoint list one row cannot hold. Serving one here would be another `parser_config` key and another expression, never a branch on what a cursor happens to look like.

### Nothing here ends the pass

`fullResponse` is on, so this node answers exactly one item per request whatever the body turned out to be. Without it a JSON array comes back as one item per element, and the node below could no longer say which source a payload came from.

`neverError` is on, so a 404 or a 500 arrives as data carrying its status, and the error output continues on the regular branch, so a refused connection, a timeout or an endpoint somebody never finished configuring arrives as an item carrying no status at all. Each of those is an outcome a source can have and each is the health group's to read. A dead source is a row to flag, not a pass to abort.

## One Row Per Distinct Item

`Write Documents` inserts one `documents` row per reading and deduplicates on `documents.hash`, so capturing the same item twice writes once. Repetition is the ordinary case rather than a fault: a poll overlaps the one before it, two feeds carry the same item, an operator re-runs a pass by hand. All three land on the row already there.

The key is a digest over the item's own url and body and nothing else. The source is deliberately left out, which is what makes a second feed carrying an item land on the first feed's row instead of beside it, and the run is left out too, so re-running a pass costs requests and no rows.

### The same digest, computed twice

`src/sources/listing-api.ts` computes this hash Node side for the adapter path, and the statement on this node computes it in SQL for this one. Two writers, one unique key. Nothing raises when the two spellings drift apart: the corpus grows a second row for every item both paths reach, and the first symptom is a count somewhere much further downstream.

### What a repeat capture does not do

It does not correct the row already standing. The stored `parse_status` and `parse_error` are the first reading's, and content that hashes the same cannot have parsed differently unless the source's `contract` moved. Moving a contract is an operator's edit, and re-reading a corpus under a new one is a pass of its own rather than a side effect of the next poll.

### What is not a document

A fetch that yielded no reading writes nothing here. That covers a `parser_config` nobody can read, a payload holding no records where the config said records would be, and a request that never completed. Each is a fact about the source rather than an item in the corpus, and the health group beside this node is what records that it happened: the counter climbs, crossing the threshold sets `sources.flagged`, and the payload itself is not kept.

## The Free Decision Runs First

Two decisions are taken between a document being written and a model being asked about it, and both are free. `Mark Near Duplicates` says whether this pass captured something the domain already has, and `Gate Documents` says whether the domain's own terms make it worth reading. Neither opens a socket and neither writes a row.

The group below this one is where a pass starts costing something. Every document that reaches it went through here first, which is what makes the ordering on this canvas a spending rule rather than a preference.

### A duplicate is marked, not dropped

`documents.hash` already refuses an item captured twice byte for byte, so what is left here is the pair that reads the same and does not hash the same: a listing that re-renders, a page that gained a timestamp, one item carried by two feeds under different wrappers. `src/lib/shingle.ts` sketches both bodies and says whether they overlap enough to be one document.

A document that converges keeps its row and carries the id of the earlier one it matched. Nothing is merged and nothing is deleted, and only the earlier row goes on to be spent on. Which pair the pass thought were the same thing stays readable afterwards, which a merge would not leave behind.

### Two things a null means here

A document nothing could be compared against is not a document unlike everything else. `src/lib/shingle.ts` refuses to judge a body too short to fill a sketch, because overlap is measured against the smaller of two sketches and a short body would otherwise read as a perfect match for any longer one containing it. That refusal arrives as a null similarity beside a compared count of zero, never as a similarity of zero.

The gate draws the same line. A document with no body to score and one in a language the term set cannot read are both parked for a person with a null score, where a confident zero would drop them.

### What a domain with no terms gets

Every document ignored. The threshold is the library's default and a term set that matches nothing scores zero against it, so a domain nobody has written `terms` rows for spends nothing at all. That is the safe direction for a gate on spending, and each document says so: the reason recorded beside it carries the score, the threshold it was compared against and that no term matched.

nodes.name: Three Rules In Front Of A Call

parameters.content:
## Three Rules In Front Of A Call

Every model call this port makes carries the same three rules, and this group is the first place they bind. A per run ceiling is declared and applied before anything is prepared. A row is written to `llm_calls` for the call that was made, charged to the run that made it. And the model node declares `retryOnFail: false`, so a call that fails is a call that happened once.

`docs/architecture/01-invariants.md` holds the three as one register row, and `tests/invariants/workflows.test.ts` reads them off the built artifact rather than off this source: a ceiling is a named constant a reviewer can find, a ledger row is an INSERT the node making the call runs, and the retry setting is a node member.

### The call goes through a model node, not an HTTP request

The endpoint speaks a chat completions API and could be reached with the same HTTP Request node this workflow already uses three groups above. It is not. A call made that way is invisible to all three guards, every one of which finds the nodes that spend by their type: a workflow spending through an ordinary API node would carry no ceiling anybody checks and no ledger row anybody misses.

### The address is a row, not a build setting

`connectors` holds one row per external service this deployment calls, and the `llm` row is where the endpoint and the model name come from. The design this port draws from read both out of an environment variable baked into the artifact at build time, so pointing the pipeline at another model meant a rebuild and a redeploy of every workflow that named it, and asking where it currently pointed meant reading the built file. Here it is an UPDATE and a SELECT.

### The persona is a row too, and it is the trusted half

A prompt is two channels here and not one string. `Prepare Model Prompt` answers the domain's own persona text and the fenced document as separate members, and the node below puts each in its own channel. Everything inside the fence is stated to be data that is read and never followed, and every active form in it is defanged on the way through. What the model is fed past that is the prepared chunk, because the body does not survive that node.

### What the ceiling drops does not come back

A document gated in and left outside the ceiling keeps its row, its score and its reason, and gains no finding. A later pass fetches the same item, the exact key on `documents.hash` recognises it, and it is not a new document any more, so nothing offers it a second time. That is why the budget is spent in score order rather than in the order the stream happened to arrive in.

nodes.name: A Refused Answer Is Not An Error

parameters.content:
## A Refused Answer Is Not An Error

This group is where a model's reply is checked against what the domain actually asked for, and where a reply that does not fit is dropped without stopping anything. `DomainSettings.fieldContract` in `src/db/schema/domains.ts` names each field a finding of this domain may carry and what it holds; `findings.fields` is where the checked payload lands.

### The contract is the enforcement, and there is no other

No CHECK reaches inside a JSONB payload, which `findings.fields` says in its own comment. So the Code node here is the whole of what stands between a model's answer and a stored finding, and everything it lets through is everything a reader of that column will ever see.

### What refuses a document, and what stops the pass

A contract nobody can read is the operator's fault, is the same fault for every document in the batch, and would otherwise be a run that spent its calls and wrote nothing: it stops the pass by name. An answer that does not fit a readable contract is one reply about one document, and it refuses that document alone. The two faults are separated the way `src/lib/parser-config.ts` separates `parserConfigErrors` from `contractErrors`.

### A refused answer leaves the document standing

The document was fetched, hashed, stored, compared against the corpus and gated before a call was made, and each of those left a row. A reply in the wrong shape says nothing about any of them, so nothing is undone: the row, the hash, the gate score and the reason all stand, and the finding is simply not made. What that costs is that the refusal is visible in this execution and in no row, and nothing offers the document again.

### Nothing quoted, nothing invented

No refusal sentence repeats a value the model wrote, the same rule `documents.parse_error` is written under and a sharper one here. And the keys stored are the contract's own, so a field the answer invented is lost rather than kept: what a domain's findings hold is the domain's declaration.

nodes.name: The Pass Says What It Did

parameters.content:
## The Pass Says What It Did

Three nodes close an ingest pass: the intentions it raised, the scoring it handed on, and the `runs` row it finishes. Everything above this point wrote about one document or one source at a time. This group is the only place that speaks about the pass as a whole.

### Noticing is not researching

`research_pool` in `src/db/schema/entities.ts` is an approval gate, and its whole argument is that noticing a subject is worth looking into and actually looking are separate events. One intention is raised per finding this pass wrote, carrying the finding's own string fields as the exact terms a search would be issued with, so an operator rules on what will be sent rather than on an account of it. A finding with nothing searchable raises nothing, and a finding another pass already queued raises nothing.

### Three columns, three questions

`runs.status` is what the pass came to, `counts` is what it did, `errors` is what it could not do. A source that failed makes the pass `partial` and appends an entry naming the row; every source failing makes it `failed`; a model answer the contract refused makes it neither, that refusal being a reply about one document and not a fault in the pass. The counts are the only durable record of two things no column holds: how many documents the free gate turned away, and how many were near duplicates.

### What the dispatcher does after

`ar-dispatch` opened this run, waits for this workflow, and then writes `status` and `finished_at` itself. So the status written here can be overwritten by an `ok` from there. What survives either way is `counts`, which nothing in `ar-dispatch` touches, and `errors`, which both sides append to rather than assign.

### The run a pass never reaches

Every node here is on one main chain, and a node handed no item does not run. A pass that selected no source, or whose gate ignored every document, stops above this group and leaves its `runs` row at the `running` default, which `ar-dispatch` cannot finish either. The repair is a branch off `Load Domain Context`, and it belongs to the canvas rather than to this group.
